demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette:
Daniel Mercer was 34, married, and working as a school counselor in a public middle school when the event that now organizes his life took place. He had been helping a student across the street from the school after dismissal when the boy suddenly darted backward into traffic. Daniel reacted on instinct, lunging to pull him out of the road, but in the scramble he shoved him hard against the curb and the child struck his head badly. The ambulance, the blood, and the look on the boy’s face stayed with Daniel in a way he could not shake. In the weeks after, anything that reminded him of that afternoon—stressful moments at work, the sterile smell of a clinic hallway, the sight of a waiting room, even the odor of antiseptic or sweat from a crowded gym—could pull him straight back into it. When those cues hit, he found himself trying to keep his mind occupied all the time, filling every silence with email, charting, errands, or podcasts, and he began avoiding police entirely, crossing streets or taking long detours if he saw a cruiser parked near the school. He also started steering clear of thinking about what happened, not trusting himself to open the memory even for a second.

What he feared most was that the event had proved something terrible about him. Daniel had come to believe that he could not trust himself to do the right thing, and that his life had been destroyed by what he had done. He blamed himself for the injury, replaying the moment his hands hit the child and telling himself that if he had acted differently, none of it would have happened. Those appraisals made ordinary reminders feel dangerous: a tense parent-teacher conference, a request from the nurse to accompany a student to a medical examination, or even a smell that resembled disinfectant could feel like confirmation that he was still living inside the aftermath. Each reminder strengthened the thought that he was the kind of person who could ruin everything in a split second, and that sense of moral failure fed the same urge to stay busy, to avoid the police, and to shut down any thought that might bring him back to the scene.

At times, the memory did not feel like a memory at all. Daniel described it as happening right now, with the curb under his shoe, the noise of the brakes, and the smell of hot pavement and blood arriving together so vividly that he could not find words for it. He knew what had happened, but when he tried to tell his wife or his therapist, the account came out broken and halting, as if language failed the moment the images became real again. Once the scene took hold, he became intensely alert, especially at night; he had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay vigilant, as if some second disaster might still be waiting. The reliving carried a force that made him physically react—his chest tightened, his stomach dropped, and he could feel his whole body bracing. And because the memory came back with such full sensory force, it deepened the belief that he had indeed caused irreversible harm, making him think again that his life was damaged beyond repair and that he could never fully trust his own judgment.

The more Daniel tried to keep the episode out of mind, the more it seemed to return in fragments. He stayed excessively occupied through the school day, answering emails long after hours and volunteering for extra tasks, but that constant distraction left him more tired and less steady. In those drained moments, the memory intruded more easily, especially when stress was high or when he caught a related smell in a school bathroom or clinic office. He noticed that his efforts to outrun the memory only made it feel closer and more imminent, as if it were waiting for any gap in his attention. His fear of that surge of feeling, and of what it would say about him, kept him on guard at night and pulled him into the same loop of self-reproach. By the time he came for help, Daniel was exhausted by the effort of staying busy, ashamed of how much he avoided police and medical settings, and frightened that one more reminder would bring the whole scene back with the same terrible certainty. What brought him in was the growing sense that he could not keep living this way, and what he wanted most was to sleep without standing guard against his own mind, though he still feared that if he let himself think about the event honestly, he would be overwhelmed by the proof that he had destroyed his own life.
